The graduate field of aerospace engineering provides a program of instruction and research in the disciplines of fluid dynamics, materials and structures, and dynamics and control, with applications to the host of engineering problems that involve the flight of vehicles in the Earth’s atmosphere and in space.

Current research projects are in such areas as computational fluid dynamics; turbulent flows and their control; space vehicle dynamics; combustion; theoretical and applied mechanics of solids and fluids; advanced composite materials; and aeroacoustics. There is close cooperation between the faculty of aerospace engineering and those in related fields, especially mechanical engineering, theoretical and applied mechanics, and electrical and computer engineering.

Students who earn a Ph.D. in aerospace engineering are prepared for leadership roles at the nation’s foremost industrial and government laboratories and as faculty members in university research and teaching.

A Ph.D. in robotics will give you the skills to create the next generation of robotics solutions to the challenges facing our world, from autonomous vehicles and exploration to manufacturing and healthcare.

The graduate field of robotics at Cornell is an interdisciplinary group of researchers working on all aspects of robotics, including perception, control, learning, planning, and human-robot interaction. Faculty and students come from many departments, including computer science, mechanical engineering, electrical and computer engineering, and aerospace engineering. A primary goal of the field is to create an environment where students can focus on robotics research, guided by faculty who are experts in robotics, in a way that is not possible within a traditional departmental structure.

The graduate field of Africana studies at Cornell has a long and distinguished history. For over forty years, the faculty has trained students who have become leading scholars in the field. The Ph.D. program in Africana studies is interdisciplinary. It aims to provide students with a firm foundation in the contested history of the field, its seminal texts, and its key concepts, theories and methods. Students will develop an understanding of the scholarly and social-movement origins of Africana studies, as well as the relationships among its diverse intellectual and political traditions. Students will also be expected to achieve depth in a specific area or topic related to the study of the African diaspora.

The field has two required courses, one in theory and method and the other in history of the field. Students can specialize in African, African-American or Caribbean studies. They also can take advantage of faculty specializations in areas such as Africana feminisms, expressive arts and literature, history, and political economy and development.

Students applying to this field are admitted to the Ph.D. program. The field does not admit students for a terminal M.A. degree.

The Master of Professional Studies (M.P.S.) in Agriculture and Life Sciences is a one-year, course-based master’s degree that prepares individuals for the workplace. The M.P.S. degree is for individuals who are interested in in-depth study in a particular academic field, but who do not wish to pursue a traditional, research-based Ph.D. The degree has a strong foundation in a specific sub-discipline, combined with structured professional development coursework and a problem-solving project instead of a thesis. The M.P.S. degree program is designed to be completed in two semesters of full-time study.

Students in the graduate field of biological and environmental engineering are part of an interdisciplinary group that applies basic sciences and engineering to living systems and the environment. Students can specialize in a variety of areas, such as bioprocess engineering, bioenvironmental engineering, sustainable energy systems, industrial biotechnology, synthetic biology, ecosystem and water-resources engineering, engineering for a circular economy, digital agriculture, waste treatment and management, soil and water bio-geochemistry and environmental management.

Coursework must be taken with at least two faculty members of the AIIS graduate field who represent at least two different fields of study. Students pursuing the AIIS minor will be part of a vibrant intellectual community that includes faculty and students from a variety of disciplines and national backgrounds. column47:
The graduate field of animal science offers M.S. and Ph.D. degree programs with a concentration in animal science. In this research-based degree program, students work with one of Cornell’s world-class faculty members and have access to state-of-the-art research facilities. Research programs in animal science apply basic and applied sciences to the study of the biology and management of domestic animals, including livestock, companion, and laboratory animals. Specific areas of research include animal genetics and genomics, animal nutrition, animal physiology, and animal welfare and management. The goal of these research programs is to improve animal productivity, health, and well-being.

Most students pursuing an M.S. or Ph.D. in animal science focus their research within one of four general areas: animal breeding and genetics, animal nutrition, animal physiology, or animal welfare and management. Research in animal breeding and genetics covers quantitative, molecular, and computational genetics and genomics and aims to improve the health and productivity of both domestic and non-domesticated species of animals. Research in animal nutrition focuses on the digestion, absorption, metabolism, and excretion of nutrients in order to improve nutrient utilization and efficiency, improve animal health, and reduce the environmental impact of animal agriculture. Research in physiology is aimed at understanding the basic biology of animals with a particular emphasis on the biology of reproduction, lactation, growth, and development. Research in animal management and welfare examines the effects of management and housing systems on animal health, well-being, and productivity, and aims to develop more sustainable animal production systems. Research in all of these areas is conducted at the whole animal, organ system, cellular, and molecular levels. Students are not restricted to one of these areas of study and can take a multi-disciplinary approach by including faculty from other areas of animal science and other graduate fields as part of their special committee.

In addition to the graduate field of animal science, other graduate fields that may be of interest to students include biomedical and biological sciences, food science and technology, and zoology and wildlife conservation.

column47: Anthropology is the comparative study of humankind, from its beginnings millions of years ago to the present day. The field of anthropology at Cornell is composed of three subfields: sociocultural anthropology, archaeology, and biological anthropology. Sociocultural anthropology is the study of contemporary human societies and cultures. Archaeology is the study of past human societies and cultures through the material remains they have left behind. Biological anthropology is the study of human and non-human primate evolution and adaptation, past and present. The graduate program is designed to provide the institutional setting, financial support, and intellectual community for developing professional competence in one of these three subfields. We encourage research that is theoretically engaged, ethnographically grounded, and interdisciplinary in nature. The program offers a Ph.D. in anthropology. Although the M.A. is not a terminal degree, students admitted to the Ph.D. program may receive an M.A. after fulfilling certain requirements.

Students entering the M.S. degree program receive a generous funding package that covers tuition and provides a stipend.

The master of professional studies (M.P.S.) degree is a one-year professional degree for students with an undergraduate degree and professional experience who are interested in enhancing their knowledge of one of the subject matter areas. A variety of concentrations are offered in each of the subject matter areas. Students have considerable flexibility in the choice of courses and are required to complete a problem-solving project advised by a faculty member.

The doctor of philosophy (Ph.D.) degree trains students for careers in research and teaching. Graduates take positions at leading academic institutions, international research centers, government agencies, non-governmental organizations, and private-sector firms. Ph.D. students work closely with AEM faculty members and often collaborate with faculty and graduate students from other fields at Cornell, such as economics, management, natural resources, policy analysis and management, and civil engineering.

The program prepares students for a variety of careers including data scientists, UX designers, product managers, technology analysts, and more.

The MPS in AIT degree program has three tracks: Information Technology, User Experience (UX) Design, and Data Science & Analytics. The curriculum is flexible, with options for students to tailor their course of study to their own interests and career goals. Students take a combination of foundational courses, specialized electives, and a capstone project. In the project, students work in teams to solve a real-world problem for a client, giving them hands-on experience and the opportunity to apply their skills in a professional setting. The program is designed for students from a variety of backgrounds, including those with degrees in computer science, engineering, business, and the humanities. column47: The graduate field of applied mathematics offers a Ph.D. and a terminal M.S. degree. Students in the Ph.D. program can pursue a concentration in either applied mathematics or operations research. The Ph.D. program is flexible and is designed to accommodate a variety of student interests. It is a research-oriented degree, and all students write a dissertation. The M.S. is a two-semester professional degree. A specific curriculum of courses provides students with a strong base in the techniques and theory of applied mathematics and operations research. This program provides excellent training for a variety of industrial and government positions. Applied mathematics is an interdisciplinary field that focuses on the creation and imaginative use of mathematical concepts to pose and solve problems over the entire gamut of the physical, biological, and social sciences, in engineering, and in finance. It is a dynamic field, which is constantly developing new mathematical tools in response to new problems and which finds new areas of application for existing mathematics. The Cornell Center for Applied Mathematics, which administers the graduate field, has 10 core faculty members and over 80 associated faculty members from 16 departments. These faculty members bring an enormous breadth and depth to the applied mathematics program. Their interests include—but are not restricted to—the areas of applied analysis, computational mathematics, dynamical systems, fluid dynamics, industrial and engineering mathematics, mathematical biology, mathematical finance, mechanics, networks, optimization, probability, and statistics.

column47: Applied Physics at Cornell is a field characterized by the application of physical principles to a variety of problems in engineering and science. The curriculum is flexible and can be adapted to individual interests. The field is composed of faculty from several departments in the College of Engineering and the College of Arts and Sciences. Research concentrations include: condensed-matter and materials physics, quantum information and quantum matter, optics and photonics, biophysics, and plasma physics. Many research projects are carried out in collaboration with the excellent interdisciplinary research centers at Cornell. Students entering the Ph.D. program should have a strong preparation in physics or a related discipline with a solid background in mathematics. Typically, during the first year of graduate study, students concentrate on their coursework and serve as teaching assistants. By the end of the first year, students usually select a thesis advisor and a research area. During the second year, coursework is generally completed, and students begin their thesis research. A qualifying examination for the Ph.D. is usually taken at the end of the second year. Students with an appropriate undergraduate degree can enter the Ph.D. program directly.

column47: Archaeology at Cornell is an interdisciplinary program, drawing faculty and students from a variety of departments in the humanities and social sciences. The Program of Archaeology is not a degree-granting department; rather, faculty members in the program belong to other departments at Cornell. Graduate students are admitted to the Graduate School through the graduate field of archaeology, and they work toward a M.A. or a Ph.D. degree in archaeology. Graduate students admitted to the program must focus on a specific area of study that is well represented by the faculty. Cornell has particular strengths in the archaeology of the following areas: the Aegean, the ancient Near East, classical Greece and Rome, Egypt, Europe, North America, Mesoamerica, South America, and South and Southeast Asia. Students should consult the list of faculty to identify those with whom they might work. Topical strengths of the program include but are not limited to archaeobotany, archaeometallurgy, bioarchaeology, ceramic analysis, dendrochronology, geoarchaeology, heritage studies, household archaeology, lithic analysis, and zooarchaeology. Graduate students must secure a commitment from at least one archaeology faculty member to serve on their special committee before they will be considered for admission to the program. The director of graduate studies in archaeology is able to help prospective students in this process. Contact information for the director of graduate studies in archaeology may be found under Contact Information on the right side of this page. Cornell has an extensive system of libraries, with holdings relevant to all areas of archaeological inquiry. The program is affiliated with the Cornell Institute of Archaeology and Material Studies (CIAMS) which provides a network for archaeological research and teaching across the university. CIAMS hosts a lecture series and a variety of workshops. It also offers support for student research and conference travel.

The Master of Science in Architectural Science is a post-professional research-based degree program with a concentration in Matter Design Computation. The program operates at the intersection of architecture, computation, engineering, and material science, and offers a framework for research as a focused and in-depth academic endeavor. The curriculum provides a solid intellectual basis for advanced and independent research, along with the development of the necessary skills for in-depth technical investigations into emerging material technologies.

The degree program is intended for applicants who hold a professional degree in architecture or related fields, and who are interested in engaging in advanced research. Matter Design Computation focuses on materials, with an emphasis on research informed by the latest manufacturing technologies and computational design techniques. A central concern is the development of innovative design and fabrication strategies for novel performative material systems in the context of architecture. This program provides students with the opportunity to pursue individualized research under the guidance of our internationally recognized faculty. The M.S. degree in Architectural Science is intended to be a terminal degree. Upon its successful completion, graduates are qualified to continue on to a Ph.D. degree or to enter the profession as specialists in practice.

HAUD has particular strengths in early modern, modern, and contemporary architecture and urbanism in a global context, with specializations in Asia, Africa, Europe, and North and Latin America. The program takes advantage of Cornell’s interdisciplinary resources, encouraging students to make connections with other fields in the humanities. HAUD prepares students for careers in research and teaching in universities, for curatorial positions in museums and archives, and for careers in architectural criticism and journalism.

column47:
The graduate field of Nutrition provides students with a strong foundation in basic and applied nutritional sciences through course work and original research in an environment of multidisciplinary collaboration. The field comprises more than 40 faculty members from 11 departments and 4 colleges, with interests spanning from the level of the molecule to that of the population. Concentrations for the M.S. and Ph.D. degrees are offered in: Molecular Nutrition, Human Nutrition, Community Nutrition, and International Nutrition.

Molecular Nutrition: This concentration focuses on the metabolic and biochemical basis of nutrition. Students in this concentration integrate the principles of genetics, biochemistry, physiology, and nutrition to understand the role of nutrients in gene expression, cell signaling, and metabolism. Research areas include nutrient-gene interactions, nutrient signaling, vitamin and mineral metabolism, nutrient bioavailability, lipid and carbohydrate metabolism, and amino acid metabolism.

Human Nutrition: This concentration emphasizes the integration of human metabolism and nutritional biochemistry. Students in this concentration gain in-depth knowledge of how nutrients and dietary patterns influence human health and disease. Research may be conducted with human subjects or in clinical settings.

Community Nutrition: This concentration focuses on human nutrition as it relates to promoting health and preventing disease in communities. Students in this concentration may focus on behavioral nutrition, nutrition intervention and policy, or epidemiology. Coursework covers nutritional sciences, statistics, human development, sociology, communication, and economics.

International Nutrition: This concentration emphasizes the nutritional problems of developing countries. Students in this concentration focus on the causes and consequences of malnutrition, and the design and evaluation of nutrition interventions at the individual, household, community, national and international levels. A unique aspect of this concentration is the summer field experience.

A unique feature of graduate study in Nutrition at Cornell is the opportunity for students to tailor their programs to their specific interests by taking courses and working with faculty in a wide range of disciplines.

The graduate field of Biomedical and Biological Sciences (BBS) is an umbrella program for the basic biomedical sciences at Cornell University. First-year BBS students have the opportunity to explore a variety of research areas before selecting a specific field of study and a thesis advisor.

Upon entering the program, students may choose to work with any of more than 160 faculty members in seven major fields of study, based at the College of Veterinary Medicine and the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences. After completing three or four lab rotations in their first year, students select a major field and a mentor. They then complete the Ph.D. degree in that major field.

The seven major fields of study are:
- Biochemistry, Molecular and Cell Biology
- Cancer Biology
- Immunology and Infectious Disease
- Microbiology
- Pharmacology
- Physiology, Biophysics, and Systems Biology
- Stem Cell Biology

The curriculum is designed to provide students with a broad knowledge of modern biomedical science, as well as an in-depth understanding of one or more of the above areas. All students are required to participate in laboratory rotations and teaching. They also participate in journal clubs and seminars. Students may earn a minor in any field offered for graduate study at Cornell. This structure offers a high degree of flexibility that allows students to tailor the program to their individual needs and interests.

The graduate field of Classics at Cornell has a long and distinguished tradition of training students for academic careers. The field offers Ph.D. degrees in five concentrations: Ancient History, Ancient Philosophy, Classical Archaeology, Classical Philology and Literature, and Indo-European Linguistics. Students are expected to complete the doctoral degree within five years.

The field combines a traditional emphasis on philological and literary training with the historical study of all aspects of the Greco-Roman world. The faculty has great strength in Greek and Latin philology, Greek and Roman history, classical art and archaeology, ancient philosophy, Greek and Roman religion, and Indo-European linguistics.

Students take advantage of formal and informal ties with several other fields and programs, including the graduate fields of History, Philosophy, and History of Art & Archaeology; the Cornell Institute of Archaeology and Material Studies (CIAMS); the Medieval Studies, Religious Studies, and Feminist, Gender, and Sexuality Studies Programs; and the Society for the Humanities. These ties make it possible to incorporate a broad range of interdisciplinary training into the curriculum.

The field also provides exceptional opportunities for professional development, including experience in teaching Latin, Greek, and other classics courses. There are numerous lecture series and colloquia at Cornell that bring in internationally-recognized scholars to speak on topics relevant to the field of Classics. Students regularly organize workshops and conferences to foster their own and their peers’ research interests and intellectual development. Resources for travel to conferences and for research are readily available from both the field and the Graduate School. In addition to a generous fellowship package that includes summer support, the field awards several prizes annually to graduate students for distinguished work in Latin, Greek, and other areas of classical studies.

Finally, the Cornell University Library is one of the world’s great research libraries.

The program is appropriate for students with interests that bridge traditional departmental boundaries and who wish to address questions that require the tools of several disciplines.

Students may choose one of five concentrations: Language and Cognition, Perception and Cognition, Cognition and Development, Computation and Cognition, and Neuroscience and Cognition. Students choose a primary mentor from the field faculty, and two minor mentors, one of whom must be from a different discipline than the primary mentor. The Ph.D. in cognitive science is intended to prepare students for a career in academic research and teaching, or for a position in the growing number of commercial enterprises that rely on cognitive science research.

The graduate minor in cognitive science is available to any student in a regular graduate degree program at Cornell.

column47: The graduate field of communication focuses on the study of communication as a social science. Students concentrate on one of the following areas: communication and technology, risk and science communication, or media communication. The graduate program emphasizes theory development and research. Research is broadly defined to include a wide array of quantitative and qualitative methods. All students are required to gain a thorough grounding in communication theory and research methods. Faculty research covers topics in communication and technology, media communication, and risk and science communication. The M.S. and Ph.D. programs offer a combination of strong disciplinary training in sociology and broad interdisciplinary study of the social, political, economic, and cultural processes that shape development.

Training can include instruction in appropriate foreign languages, econometrics and other advanced quantitative methods, qualitative methods, and geographic information systems. A major strength of the program is the opportunity for students to work closely with a Special Committee of faculty members chosen by the student to represent his or her major and minor fields of study. The graduate field of development sociology has a long and distinguished history of research, teaching, and service around the world. Faculty are committed to engaged research that addresses major global challenges. With a strong tradition of international and domestic research, development sociology is concerned with the causes and consequences of social and economic change, and the linkages of the local and the global. Specific faculty research interests include a range of topics in the areas of international and domestic development, demography, environment and natural resources, and rural and agricultural change. Research and teaching are organized around three concentrations: 1) states, markets, and institutions; 2) population and development; and 3) sociology of development. Faculty also direct the Community and Regional Development Institute (CaRDI) and are affiliated with several area studies programs.

The field offers a Ph.D. in development sociology. The Ph.D. program is research-oriented, and students work closely with faculty in their areas of specialization. The program provides strong training in sociological theory and research methods as they apply to development studies. Most students conduct field research for their dissertations, and the program has an excellent record of placing its graduates in academic and research positions in the U.S. and around the world. For students seeking a practice-oriented degree, the Department of Global Development offers a professional master’s degree program (M.P.S.) in global development.

Research strengths in the field include the following: the cognitive, social, emotional, and biological aspects of development; the influence of social and cultural contexts (e.g., family, peers, school, community, culture) on development; and the role of developmental processes in the etiology of psychopathology, risk, and resilience. column47: Developmental psychology is the scientific study of how and why individuals change over the course of their lives. Originally concerned with infants and children, the field has expanded to include adolescence, adult development, aging, and the entire lifespan. This field examines change across a broad range of topics including motor skills and other psycho-physiological processes; cognitive development involving areas such as problem solving, moral understanding, and conceptual understanding; language acquisition; social, personality, and emotional development; and self-concept and identity formation. Students are also encouraged to participate in one or more of the several interdisciplinary programs on campus, including the Cognitive Studies Program and the Cornell Institute for Public Affairs. Close ties are maintained with faculty members in other fields, including those in the other psychology departments, Human Development, Neurobiology and Behavior, and the Division of Nutritional Sciences. Faculty and students often collaborate with colleagues from the Weill Cornell Medical College.

They are admitted to study in the field of East Asian literature as a whole, and declare a major and two minor areas of concentration at the end of their first year of study. Possible major concentrations are Chinese literature, Japanese literature, and Korean literature. Minor concentrations are chosen from a list of options that includes a second East Asian literature, as well as a range of other possibilities such as anthropology, art history, comparative literature, feminist, gender & sexuality studies, film, history, linguistics, performing and media arts, and religious studies. In all cases, a student’s course of study is organized in close consultation with the Special Committee. The program of study is administered by the Department of Asian Studies.

The graduate field of ecology and evolutionary biology is a large, diverse, and collaborative group of faculty and graduate students studying a wide range of topics and organisms in ecology and evolutionary biology. Students in the graduate program in EEB may pursue studies at the M.S. or Ph.D. level. Students are trained in the broad disciplines of ecology and evolutionary biology. They learn the fundamentals of the scientific process from the generation of research questions and hypotheses to the design of empirical studies and the analysis and interpretation of data. Students are exposed to the breadth of research in ecology and evolutionary biology through seminars and journal clubs and become experts in their own research areas.

The Field of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology offers M.S. and Ph.D. degrees. The M.S. degree is generally awarded to students as a step toward earning a Ph.D., and very few students are admitted to the field for a terminal M.S. degree. Prospective M.S. students are encouraged to contact EEB faculty to inquire about opportunities in their labs.

The graduate field of ecology and evolutionary biology includes more than 100 faculty from 17 departments in six colleges, plus the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and the Boyce Thompson Institute. We are united by an interest in ecology and evolution and a desire to train the next generation of leaders in these areas. The field is broadly organized into eight graduate concentrations: Animal Behavior; Chemical Ecology; Community and Ecosystem Ecology; Environmental and Organismal Biology; Evolutionary Genetics and Genomics; Evolutionary Patterns and Processes; Plant Biology; and Sustainable Development. Each is an intellectual hub for faculty and students with shared interests. Most faculty and students identify with more than one concentration.

Students may pursue either a M.S. or a Ph.D. degree. The Ph.D. is a research degree requiring an original contribution to science. The M.S. is also a research degree; it may be an appropriate goal for students who have not had a great deal of research experience, or for students whose career plans require a M.S. but not a Ph.D.

All students work closely with a Special Committee of three or four faculty members who help guide the student’s graduate education and research. The committee must include at least one member from each of two graduate concentrations. One member of the committee may be from outside the field of EEB. Students also may have an unofficial advisor on their committee from a cooperating institution, such as the American Museum of Natural History.

Most graduate students in the field of ecology and evolutionary biology receive financial support in the form of fellowships, research assistantships, and/or teaching assistantships. The support package includes tuition, a stipend, and health insurance.

The graduate program in economics at Cornell is a Ph.D. program that trains students to be leaders in economic research. Cornell’s Ph.D. program in economics is a research degree and is usually pursued by students who wish to do the kind of research done by academic economists.

The doctoral program in economics has two stages. The first is a two-year sequence of courses that provides rigorous training in economic theory and econometrics. In this period, students acquire the essential tools to do economic research. Students must pass comprehensive examinations in microeconomics and macroeconomics at the end of their first year and an econometrics comprehensive exam at the beginning of their second year. After successfully completing two years of course work, students are admitted to candidacy for the Ph.D. degree.

The second stage of the program is the thesis, or dissertation, which is a significant piece of independent research. In this stage, the student works closely with his or her Special Committee. Students are required to present a research paper (known as the “A Exam” or Admission to Candidacy Examination) in their third year of study. They must complete the dissertation and defend it in an oral examination (the “B Exam”). The final examination is an oral defense of the thesis. Most students complete their doctoral studies in five years.

column47: The graduate program in English at Cornell has long been recognized as one of the best in the country, and we are committed to keeping it that way. We have a large and diverse graduate faculty with a wide range of theoretical and critical interests. The graduate program includes about 60 students in the Ph.D. program and another 12 in the M.F.A. program in Creative Writing. We offer a fully-funded Ph.D. program that admits 8-10 students a year with a six-year package of support. A relatively small program, we pride ourselves on a consistent record of placing our students in academic positions. Our program has been ranked among the top programs by the National Research Council (NRC). The field has strengths in all of the traditional historical periods of English and American literature. At the same time, we have a strong and growing commitment to the fields of post-colonial studies, minority literatures, and cultural studies. Students can take courses in and work with faculty in other departments such as Comparative Literature, the Society for the Humanities, Romance Studies, German Studies, Government, History, and History of Art, as well as in interdisciplinary programs such as Feminist, Gender, and Sexuality Studies; Medieval Studies; and Visual Culture. Close interaction among faculty and students is a key feature of our program; a lively conference and colloquium series as well as more informal events provide a sense of intellectual community. We encourage you to contact faculty in your fields of interest. We invite you to experience the intellectual excitement and rigor of a first-rate graduate program.

The field of entomology has a long and distinguished history at Cornell, beginning with the appointment of John Henry Comstock in 1872. Today, the field includes more than 30 faculty members from the departments of Entomology, Neurobiology and Behavior, Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, and Molecular Biology and Genetics. The field has particular strength in the areas of systematics and evolutionary biology, ecology, behavior, chemical ecology, molecular entomology and genomics, insect pathology, integrated pest management, medical and veterinary entomology, and apiculture. Facilities include the Cornell University Insect Collection, with more than 7 million specimens; the Page Honey Bee Research Laboratory; modern laboratories for research in all aspects of entomology; an extensive entomological library; and access to a variety of natural areas for field research. Graduate students are encouraged to select a research topic prior to or shortly after arrival on campus and to select a Special Committee of three or four faculty members that represents the student’s specific interests. Students are admitted to the field and not to the laboratory of an individual faculty member. Funding in the form of teaching or research assistantships or fellowships is available to most students.

Graduate studies in FSAD integrate knowledge from the physical and social sciences as well as art and design to create innovative and sustainable solutions that address the needs of the individual, family, and society. The field offers a multidisciplinary program with strong roots in polymer science, engineering, chemistry, physics, materials science, anthropology, economics, sociology, design, and art. Current research topics include: design processes for functional and expressive apparel and other products, including design for specific user groups, and the integration of smart technologies in textile-based products; the engineering of fibrous materials for a variety of end uses; the study of polymeric materials for fiber applications including biopolymers and green composites; the investigation of sustainable practices for the apparel and textile industry; and historical and cultural aspects of textiles and apparel.

The graduate field of Fiber Science and Apparel Design (FSAD) leads to M.S. and Ph.D. degrees and prepares students for careers in academia, government, and industry. In both programs, students choose a major subject area and two minor subjects. Study in the field of FSAD offers a unique experience integrating design, art, biology, chemistry, engineering, and social sciences to address emerging challenges in the field of textiles and apparel. The field has three major areas of specialization: fiber science, textile technology, and apparel design.

In addition, the field offers a master of professional studies (M.P.S.) in Human Ecology. This one-year, course-based master’s degree prepares individuals for leadership roles in various professions. Students complete a capstone project in lieu of a research thesis.

Cornell is an internationally recognized leader in the field of fiber science. Research encompasses the study of the physical and chemical properties of fibrous materials, the development of new fibers and fibrous systems, and the application of new technologies to the creation of innovative materials and products.

The study of apparel design focuses on the complex process by which apparel products are conceived, produced, and marketed in the context of a global fashion industry. A wide range of courses are offered to provide a strong foundation in the basic sciences and to allow for specialization. Students can select a concentration in food science or food technology. Research programs are available in food chemistry, food microbiology, food engineering, food processing, dairy science, enology, food quality, sensory evaluation, food toxicology, and international food science.

column47: The graduate field of genetics, genomics and development (GGD) is composed of 50 faculty members from 11 departments in five colleges at the Ithaca campus and the Medical College in New York City. The research interests of the GGD faculty span the breadth of modern genetics and genomics, including the areas of molecular genetics, developmental genetics, evolutionary genetics, population genetics, computational genetics, and genomics. The organisms under study include viruses, bacteria, protists, fungi, plants, and animals (including humans). GGD is a diverse and exciting field that provides unusually broad research and training opportunities. A common theme in the field of GGD is the use of genetic, genomic, and developmental approaches to understand fundamental biological questions. The field’s major strengths lie in the study of developmental genetics, evolutionary genetics and genomics, and systems biology.

column47: The graduate field of genetics, genomics and development (GGD) is a campus-wide community of faculty and graduate students with primary research interests in the areas of genetics, genomics, molecular, cellular, and developmental biology. The field brings together faculty from several colleges and departments to create a collaborative and supportive research and training environment. The primary objective of the field is to provide a training program that is flexible and tailored to the individual needs of students who wish to pursue a research career in these disciplines. Students affiliate with a particular concentration by their second year of study. Concentrations include genetics and genomics; developmental biology; and computational and statistical genomics. The GGD curriculum is similarly flexible to accommodate students with diverse interests. In the first year, students take courses and carry out three rotations in different faculty laboratories to find the ideal match for their interests. Throughout their time in the program, students take additional specialized courses related to their research, have opportunities to assist with undergraduate teaching, and participate in a rich environment of weekly seminar series, journal clubs, and retreats. Students are also encouraged to travel to national and international meetings, as well as other scientific conferences where they present their work.

The graduate field of geological sciences is composed of faculty from the Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences. Research in geological sciences at Cornell covers a wide spectrum, ranging from the deep earth to its surface and from billion-year-old rocks to active volcanoes. Cornell geoscientists are engaged in research all over the world, with especially active programs in the Andes, the Pacific, the Caribbean, the Middle East, and the American West. Graduate study in geology, geobiology, geophysics, geochemistry, and geohydrology is conducted in a stimulating atmosphere of departmental seminars, informal discussion groups, and close student-faculty interaction.

column47: The Master of Professional Studies (M.P.S.) in Global Development is an interdisciplinary, one-year, course-based master’s degree that prepares individuals for careers in international development. Through a combination of coursework and an intensive, hands-on capstone project, you’ll develop the knowledge and skills to lead change, create more equitable and sustainable communities and make a difference in the world. As a student in our program, you will join a diverse cohort of experienced professionals and emerging leaders from around the globe. Coursework will equip you with a foundational understanding of development theory, policy and practice, as well as specialized knowledge in your chosen concentration area. The main objective of our M.P.S. program is to train skilled, thoughtful and effective development practitioners who are equipped to address the world’s most pressing challenges. Our program provides a solid foundation for careers in a wide range of fields, including international agriculture and rural development, community and economic development, development policy, social justice and equity, environmental protection and program planning, management and evaluation.

The graduate field of global development offers M.S. and Ph.D. degree programs that are broadly concerned with the challenges of international development. Within the M.S. degree program, students specialize in either Development Sociology or International Agriculture and Rural Development. Students interested in the Ph.D. program should refer to the graduate field of development sociology.

Students take a multidisciplinary approach to the study of social, political, economic, and environmental change in the global South. The program offers a strong theoretical and research-based course of study and prepares students for careers in research, policy analysis, and university-level teaching.

Students who elect to study Development Sociology are asked to concentrate in one of the following areas: states, markets, and institutions, or social and political change. Within those areas, students may choose to focus on a particular topic such as community and local development, gender, political economy, population and development, rural sociology, or environment and development. Students choosing to study International Agriculture and Rural Development are encouraged to combine interests in the social sciences with a strong grounding in at least one technical field related to agriculture and rural development.

column47: The graduate field of global development is a premier, world-renowned center for research and graduate training on processes of social, economic, political, and environmental change at the local, national and global scales. The field is problem-focused, interdisciplinary, and empirically-grounded, with a particular emphasis on the challenges of development in the Global South. Faculty affiliated with the field are drawn from a wide range of disciplines across the social and natural sciences. Students pursuing a Ph.D. in global development must complete a major in development sociology and may choose a minor from one of the other three concentrations in the field or from one of the many other graduate fields at Cornell. The field offers four concentrations: development policy and practice; development sociology; international agriculture and rural development; and international nutrition. Most students complete a significant part of their dissertation research outside the United States; research may be undertaken on the Cornell campus or at one of our many international partner institutions.

The program provides a broad education in the substance and methods of political science, and it supports students to develop their own specialized research agendas. The faculty’s research interests are highly diverse and interdisciplinary, and students can find support for a wide range of research projects. The field has particular strengths in American politics, comparative politics, political theory and international relations. Its faculty also have expertise in a wide range of interdisciplinary areas, such as political economy, political behavior, law and politics, and race and ethnicity.

column47: The graduate field of Historic Preservation Planning (HPP) offers a two-year master of arts (M.A.) degree. HPP is the only historic preservation program in the United States that is part of a department of city and regional planning and a college of architecture, art, and planning. As a result, the field takes a comprehensive, interdisciplinary approach to preservation that encompasses history and theory, planning, conservation, design, economics, law, and technology. The program offers students the opportunity to learn from and work with faculty members who have expertise in a broad range of related areas, including architectural conservation, preservation planning, landscape preservation, urban history, and real estate. Students may earn a concentration in either preservation planning, historic conservation, or real estate.

column47: The graduate program in the History of Art and Archaeology is designed to provide students with a comprehensive knowledge of the history, theory, and criticism of art. column46: Horticultural Biology, Horticultural Crop Production Systems, Public Garden Leadership
column47: The graduate field of horticulture is a multi-disciplinary program that addresses the art, science, technology, and business of plant cultivation. As a horticulture graduate student at Cornell, you will be well-positioned to tackle complex agricultural challenges including food and nutritional security, health and well-being, and environmental sustainability. From developing new fruit and vegetable varieties to managing landscapes and turfgrass, from creating better production systems for food and ornamental crops to improving post-harvest handling and storage, our faculty are leaders in their disciplines and work at the cutting-edge of plant science research. Our faculty are based in the School of Integrative Plant Science on the Ithaca campus, and at Cornell AgriTech in Geneva, NY. Students can select from a diversity of research topics including plant breeding and genetics, genomics, plant physiology, controlled environment agriculture (CEA), public garden leadership, international agriculture, post-harvest biology, turfgrass science, and production, marketing, and business management of horticultural crops. Research may be conducted in labs, greenhouses, farms, or with communities, in both local and global settings. Our graduates go on to successful careers in academia, industry, government, and for non-profit organizations in the U.S. and around the world.

column46: ['Horticultural Plant Breeding and Genetics', 'Horticultural Plant Physiology and Ecology', 'Horticultural Crop Production and Management']
column47: The graduate field of horticulture provides an integrated course of study in the biology and technology of horticultural crops (fruits, vegetables, and landscape plants). The graduate faculty has expertise in a wide range of disciplines that span the biological and environmental sciences. Research areas include plant breeding and genetics, genomics, plant physiology, plant-microbe interactions, postharvest biology, sustainable and organic production systems, and controlled-environment agriculture. Students have access to outstanding research facilities, including state-of-the-art laboratories and growth chambers, extensive germplasm collections, and several research farms.

column46: Aging & Health; Cognitive Development; Law, Psychology, & Human Development; Social & Personality Development
column47: The graduate field of Human Development offers M.A. and Ph.D. degree programs that focus on the psychological, social, and biological development of people and families across the life-span. Students in human development have excellent opportunities to form interdisciplinary collaborations with faculty and other students throughout the College of Human Ecology and Cornell University, including those in the fields of psychology, sociology, and neurobiology and behavior, as well as the Cornell Law School, and Weill Cornell Medical College. All students receive a strong theoretical and methodological grounding to do their research in one or more of the core areas of developmental psychology. In addition, students have the opportunity to take part in two training grants: one on the developmental psychobiology of stress and one on aging.

column47: The graduate field of human development offers a Ph.D. program that gives students a strong foundation in the theories and research of human development while also allowing them to specialize in an area of their own interest. Students are admitted to the field of human development as a whole, rather than to a particular professor’s lab. All students must complete four semesters of proseminar courses, as well as several advanced seminars and statistics classes. Students in human development specialize in one of five concentrations: Aging and Health; Cognitive Development; Developmental Behavioral Neuroscience; Law and Human Development; or Social and Personality Development. Students begin research in their first semester and must complete both a second-year research project and a dissertation. The majority of our graduates obtain positions in academic or research settings.

The Master of Professional Studies (M.P.S.) in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) is a one-year, two-semester program that prepares students to design, build, and evaluate the user-facing technologies of the future. The M.P.S. in HCI is based in the field of Information Science. HCI students learn from, and are part of, the broad and deep HCI community at Cornell University.

HCI is the study and practice of designing effective, usable, and satisfying interactive systems. The interdisciplinary field of HCI lies at the intersection of engineering, computer science, behavioral science, and design. Effective HCI requires a mix of technical skills (prototyping, evaluation) and communication skills (explaining and defending one’s work).

column46: A.I.D.S., Bacteriology, Cellular Immunology, Clinical Immunology, Comparative Immunology, Genetic and Molecular Immunology, Immunopathology, Parasitology, Tumor Immunology, Virology, Zoo and Wildlife Medicine
column47: The graduate field of Immunology and Infectious Disease (IID) provides outstanding training for students interested in the function of the immune system and the pathogens that subvert it. The IID field brings together faculty from five departments within the College of Veterinary Medicine and two departments at the Ithaca campus of Weill Cornell Medicine to provide a broad and rigorous educational experience that leads to the M.S. and Ph.D. degrees in immunology. The goal of the IID field is to provide state-of-the-art training in the concepts and techniques of immunology and host-pathogen interactions. The curriculum is designed to be flexible, so that each student’s course of study can be tailored to their individual needs and interests. Formal coursework is combined with extensive training in research in the laboratory of one of the graduate faculty.

column46: Bacteriology, Immunology, Parasitology, Virology, Zoology and Wildlife Conservation
column47: The graduate field of Immunology and Infectious Disease provides interdisciplinary training in the overlapping disciplines of immunology and infection biology, with an emphasis on the basic mechanisms of host-pathogen interactions. The goal of the field is to train the next generation of scientists who will contribute to the understanding and prevention of infectious and inflammatory diseases of animals and humans. The graduate program includes formal course work, journal clubs and research seminars, and original dissertation research. Trainees also develop professional skills such as scientific writing, oral presentation, and networking, which will enable them to succeed in the scientific careers of their choice. Research in the field covers a broad spectrum, including studies of viral, bacterial, and parasitic pathogens; innate and adaptive immunity; the microbiome; and immune-mediated diseases. State-of-the-art facilities and equipment for cell biology, flow cytometry, genomics, and imaging are available. Students choose their Special Committee chair from among over 30 faculty members who participate in the field. Thesis research is performed in the faculty member’s laboratory.

column46: ['Dispute Resolution', 'Human Resources and Organizations', 'International and Comparative Labor', 'Labor Market Policy', 'Labor Relations', 'Organizational Behavior']
column47: The MILR is an interdisciplinary, two-year, professional master’s degree program that provides students with a broad, problem-solving perspective on the world of work and labor. Students have the opportunity to take courses on a variety of subjects within the field of industrial and labor relations, including human resource management, labor relations, dispute resolution, labor economics, organizational behavior, international and comparative labor, and labor law and history. Graduates of the program excel in a variety of careers in business, government, labor unions, and non-profit organizations. Students gain an understanding of how to manage people and organizations; motivate employees; resolve workplace disputes; develop effective negotiating skills; formulate compensation and benefit policies; and analyze labor market trends.

The Master of Professional Studies in Industrial and Labor Relations (M.P.S.) is a one-year, full-time program based in Ithaca, New York, that provides a solid foundation in the various areas of industrial and labor relations. It is designed for practitioners with at least seven to ten years of experience in the various areas of human resources and labor relations. The program prepares students for a variety of positions in business and industry in the United States and abroad. The core courses cover labor relations, human resources, labor economics, organizational behavior, and statistics. Additional elective courses may be taken in these and other areas of the ILR School and elsewhere in the university. A major research paper or project is required.

column47:
The graduate field of Industrial and Labor Relations (ILR) provides a select group of students with an opportunity to pursue advanced study in a variety of specializations within the field. The ILR School offers four graduate degrees: the Master of Industrial and Labor Relations (M.I.L.R.), the Master of Professional Studies (M.P.S.), the Master of Science (M.S.), and the Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.).

The M.S. and Ph.D. degree programs are research-focused and designed to train students for academic and research careers. Students in these programs choose to specialize in one of five concentrations: Human Resources and Organizations, International and Comparative Labor, Labor Relations, Labor Economics, and Social Statistics. The M.I.L.R. and M.P.S. degrees are professional master’s degrees, designed to prepare students for careers as practitioners.

column47: The graduate field of Industrial and Labor Relations offers M.S. and Ph.D. degrees, with majors in five areas: human resource studies, international and comparative labor, labor economics, labor relations, law and history, and organizational behavior. Students in the M.I.L.R. program pursue a professional master’s degree. The Ph.D. program prepares students for careers as researchers and teachers in universities and research institutions. The M.S. program also is a research-oriented degree, which may be treated as a terminal degree or as the first two years of a doctoral program. The field has about seventy-five faculty members drawn from the School of Industrial and Labor Relations, and the Colleges of Arts and Sciences, and Human Ecology.

The Master of Professional Studies (M.P.S.) in Information Science is a one-year, course-based master’s degree that prepares students for careers as information science professionals. The M.P.S. is offered on the Cornell Ithaca campus and at the Cornell Tech campus in New York City. The Ithaca M.P.S. is a flexible program that allows students to focus on one of many information science sub-fields, including user experience design, data science, and interactive technologies. The Cornell Tech M.P.S. is a more structured program focused on building technology for startups and large companies that provides intensive training in technical systems building and entrepreneurship. More information on the Ithaca-based M.P.S. can be found at the Information Science M.P.S. site. More information on the Cornell Tech M.P.S. can be found at the Cornell Tech site.

column47: The graduate field of Information Science (IS) at Cornell is an interdisciplinary field that addresses the design and use of information systems in a social context. It studies the creation, representation, organization, application, and analysis of information in digital form. The field’s research and teaching are organized into three main hubs that reflect its intellectual core: human computer interaction and design; social and behavioral science; and information, data and society. The hubs integrate methods from computer science, data science, communication, design, law, and sociology. As a discipline, it grew from a confluence of interests among these several academic fields. Students in Information Science are expected to master a core of interdisciplinary material and also to develop a focus in a particular subfield.

column47: The master of professional studies (M.P.S.) is a one-year, course-based master’s degree that prepares students for the workplace. The program is ideal for career-changers and recent graduates who want to enter the workforce in an area of agriculture and life sciences. The M.P.S. in Integrative Plant Science program provides students with a graduate-level curriculum focused on the science, management, and policy issues in plant science. Students take courses in the Cornell Graduate School, and may choose from a wide array of options offered throughout the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS). The M.P.S. program is distinguished by its capstone project. Instead of a thesis, students complete a project that solves a problem and addresses an issue relevant to the professional world. Projects can be research-based, but are often in the form of internships, curriculum development, extension programs, or in-depth case studies.

The graduate field of landscape architecture offers two distinct professional master’s degree programs that are nationally accredited by the American Society of Landscape Architects: the first-professional Master of Landscape Architecture (M.L.A. AP) degree and the post-professional Master of Landscape Architecture (M.L.A.) degree. Additionally, the field offers a Master of Professional Studies (M.P.S.) in landscape architecture.

Cornell's Master of Landscape Architecture (M.L.A.) programs prepare students for professional practice and to be leaders in the field. Students explore an array of contemporary and emerging landscape architecture issues, including the relationship between urbanization and ecology, the remaking of post-industrial and post-agricultural landscapes, the challenges of climate change, the role of social and environmental justice, and the importance of ecological democracy. The programs emphasize the art and science of landscape architecture in order to create regenerative landscapes that are not only beautiful, vibrant, and resilient, but also meaningful.

The curriculum is structured in a sequence that equips students with the core knowledge and skills of the discipline while allowing for intellectual and design exploration. Studio is the core of the M.L.A. programs, where students learn to synthesize cultural and ecological systems to create new landscape forms and experiences. Studios are complemented by lectures and seminars that provide in-depth instruction in landscape history and theory, representation, techniques and technologies, and ecological and social processes. The programs engage a range of landscapes, including cities, suburbs, working landscapes, and wildlands.

Cornell's Ithaca campus, with its striking topography, deep gorges, and rich architectural and landscape history, provides an inspirational setting for this work. The expansive Cornell Botanic Gardens, which are located adjacent to the landscape architecture studios, provide an outdoor classroom for learning.

column46: ['The regular M.P.S. track', 'The Advanced Landscape Studies track']
column47:
The one-year Master of Professional Studies (M.P.S.) in Landscape Architecture is an intensive, post-professional degree for those who already have a degree in landscape architecture (B.L.A. or M.L.A.).

The M.P.S. in Landscape Architecture program offers two tracks:

1. The regular M.P.S. track is for individuals who hold an accredited degree in landscape architecture and who wish to specialize in a particular aspect of the field. Potential specializations are unlimited, but often focus on areas such as cultural landscape studies, advanced digital applications, ecological design and restoration, representation, and urbanism.
2. The Advanced Landscape Studies track is for individuals with a landscape architecture degree (or its equivalent) from a foreign institution and a minimum of three years of professional experience who are seeking to augment their knowledge of American practice. This track is not intended to be a path to licensure.

M.P.S. candidates create a highly individualized program of study that is structured by a core design studio, two required landscape architecture seminars, and a capstone project. In addition, candidates take a wide range of elective courses from across the university that are aligned with their particular focus.

The M.P.S. degree is a STEM-designated program in Architectural and Building Sciences/Technology (CIP code 04.0902).

The concurrent degree program in landscape architecture and regional planning provides an opportunity for a student to earn two degrees in a compressed timeframe. Graduates are prepared for professional careers in which design and planning are integrated, for example, in public agencies and private consulting firms that engage in master planning, environmental analysis, site design, urban design, and community development. The program also provides a strong foundation for doctoral studies in either field. The concurrent degree program is coordinated by a joint faculty committee from the two fields. Students must be accepted for admission by both the Graduate Field of Landscape Architecture and the Graduate Field of City and Regional Planning. Students may apply for admission to the concurrent degree program at the time of their initial application to the Graduate School or, for those already enrolled in one of the two fields, at any time during their first two semesters of study.

column47: The graduate minor in Latin American and Caribbean Studies is a formal academic credential designed for graduate and professional students who have a significant interest in Latin America and the Caribbean but are concentrating in another discipline. Candidates for this degree are admitted only under special circumstances. Applicants must hold a first degree in law and an LL.M. or a comparable degree. The graduate field of linguistics at Cornell is a vibrant intellectual community where faculty and graduate students work together on a wide range of topics in theoretical and experimental linguistics. The field’s core strengths are in phonetics/phonology, syntax, and semantics/pragmatics, with additional areas of specialization including historical linguistics, language acquisition, computational linguistics, and psycholinguistics.

Research in the graduate field of linguistics is characterized by a commitment to theoretically-informed empirical investigation based on a diverse range of languages. Many members of the field are also active participants in one or more of the university’s interdisciplinary programs, including Cognitive Science, Computing and Information Science, and area studies programs (e.g., East Asia Program, Southeast Asia Program, South Asia Program).

column47: The graduate field of Materials Science and Engineering (MSE) at Cornell is an interdisciplinary community of faculty, staff, and students from seven departments in the College of Engineering and the College of Arts and Sciences. The field offers M.S. and Ph.D. degree programs that provide students with a broad education in the fundamental science and engineering of materials. Students also have the opportunity to engage in focused research programs in a number of materials sub-disciplines, including biomaterials, ceramics, composites, electronic materials, metals, and polymers.

column47: The graduate field of materials science and engineering at Cornell is a Ph.D.-granting program that attracts students from a wide range of science and engineering disciplines including materials science, chemistry, physics, and mechanical, chemical, electrical and civil engineering. The field offers a flexible, interdisciplinary program, leading to M.S. and Ph.D. degrees that can be tailored to a student’s specific interests. Emphasis is on the generic science of materials that underlies a wide range of engineering applications, from information technology to biotechnology to energy technology. The field also provides a materials science and engineering minor for students outside the field. A diverse and distinguished faculty of more than 40 members offers research opportunities in a broad range of topics. These include: ceramics, complex fluids, composites, electronic materials, metals, and polymers for a wide variety of applications. Students also have access to the world-class characterization and fabrication facilities of the Cornell Center for Materials Research, the Cornell NanoScale Science & Technology Facility, the Cornell High Energy Synchrotron Source, and the Center for Advanced Computing.

The graduate program in mathematics at Cornell is a Ph.D. program. Cornell does not offer a master’s degree in mathematics as a terminal degree.

The mathematics program is organized into eight concentrations, corresponding to the main research areas of the department: algebra, analysis, combinatorics, geometry, logic, number theory, probability theory, and topology. Students may switch concentrations at any time.

The program includes a series of introductory courses, advanced topics courses, and research seminars. It is designed so that a typical student will have an advisor and be working on a thesis problem by the end of the second year.

Almost all students are supported as teaching assistants for four semesters. This includes a stipend, a full tuition fellowship, and health insurance. In later years, most students are supported as research assistants.

column47: The graduate field of mechanical engineering encompasses the fundamental thermal and fluid sciences, as well as the design, analysis, and manufacture of mechanical systems. Students may focus their studies and research in a variety of areas. The M.S. program is a research-based degree that requires completion of a thesis. Some students enter the M.S. program with the intention of continuing on to a Ph.D. A typical M.S. program requires two years of full-time study.

column46: ['Biomechanics', 'Dynamics, Controls, and Robotics', 'Energy and Sustainability', 'Fluid Mechanics', 'Materials Processing', 'Mechanics of Materials', 'Thermal Sciences', 'Transportation']
column47: The graduate field of mechanical engineering offers a broad program of study and research in a variety of areas, including: biomechanics; dynamics, controls, and robotics; energy and sustainability; fluid mechanics; materials processing; mechanics of materials; thermal sciences; and transportation. Research is directed toward a Ph.d. or an M.S. degree. There also is a professional Master of Engineering (M.Eng.) degree program.

column46: ['Islamic Studies', 'Medieval and Early Modern Studies']
column47: The graduate field of Medieval Studies offers a Ph.D. degree program that provides students with a thorough grounding in the intellectual and material cultures of medieval Europe as well as in the methods and theories of contemporary medieval scholarship. The program’s flexible structure encourages interdisciplinary work. The field brings together more than 30 faculty members from over a dozen departments in the humanities and social sciences. Core faculty in the field represent a broad geographical, chronological, and methodological range, and their courses cover all periods of medieval history and many vernacular languages and literatures, including Old and Middle English, Old Norse, medieval French, Occitan, medieval German, medieval Italian, medieval Spanish, and medieval Welsh. In addition, graduate students in Medieval Studies have direct access to Cornell’s outstanding collections of medieval manuscripts and rare books, which include the Dante and Petrarch collections, the Witchcraft Collection, the Fiske Icelandic Collection, and the Bodman Collection of Coptic manuscripts.

column47:
The graduate field of microbiology at Cornell has a long and distinguished history. It is one of the few fields in the country that spans the study of the three domains of life: bacteria, archaea, and eukarya. More than 60 faculty from 16 departments in six colleges across the Ithaca campus are members of the graduate field, providing students with a broad choice of research areas and mentors.

Students apply to the field of microbiology and not to a specific faculty member. During the first semester, students attend a series of faculty talks and perform three laboratory rotations, which provide a broad exposure to the research opportunities in the field. At the end of the first semester, students select a major professor and a research area for their dissertation work.

Research in microbiology at Cornell uses state-of-the-art approaches to study fundamental problems in bacteriology, eukaryotic microbiology, immunology and microbial pathogenesis, microbial biochemistry and physiology, microbial genetics and genomics, virology, and environmental microbiology. Modern biology has been revolutionized by genomic science, and research in microbiology has moved from the study of single genes or proteins to a systems biology approach, in which the goal is to understand how all the parts work together to make the whole. At Cornell, students in microbiology are immersed in a rich and supportive research and training environment where they can apply genomic, proteomic, and bioinformatic approaches to the study of microorganisms. This systems approach is not restricted to any one group of microorganisms, but instead is a unifying theme that ties together the diverse research interests of the faculty in the field.

column47: The graduate field of microbiology at Cornell has a long and distinguished history. Members of the field represent a broad range of interests within the discipline, from the fundamental aspects of microbial physiology, genetics, and development to the applied aspects of bioremediation, plant pathology, and industrial biotechnology. Faculty are drawn from several departments, primarily the Department of Microbiology, which resides in the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences and the College of Arts and Sciences. Faculty are also drawn from the College of Engineering and the College of Veterinary Medicine.

column46: ['Developmental Physiology', 'Endocrinology', 'Molecular and Cell Physiology', 'Neurophysiology', 'Nutritional Physiology', 'Systems and Integrative Physiology']
column47: The graduate field of molecular and integrative physiology offers programs of study leading to the M.S. and Ph.D. degrees. The field has an exceptionally broad range of research interests, and areas of focus are loosely grouped into the following categories: endocrinology; systems and integrative physiology; cell, molecular, and developmental physiology; and neurophysiology. Students may work with faculty in the College of Veterinary Medicine, the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, the College of Arts and Sciences, and the College of Engineering. Prospective students apply for admission to the field as a whole and select a special committee chair and research area during the first semester.

column46: Cellular and Molecular Physiology, Endocrinology and Reproductive Physiology, Systems Physiology
column47:
The graduate field of molecular and integrative physiology offers a broad interdisciplinary program of study leading to the Ph.D. degree. The faculty is drawn from eight departments in the College of Veterinary Medicine, College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, College of Arts and Sciences, and College of Engineering.

Research training is offered in the general areas of cellular and molecular physiology, endocrinology and reproductive physiology, and systemic physiology. The field is organized to provide maximum flexibility in the design of student programs. The selection of a special committee is of paramount importance. Normally this committee consists of the thesis adviser and two or three other faculty members who represent the student’s major and minor areas of interest. Course work is determined by the student and their special committee and is tailored to the individual’s background, interests, and needs.

All students are required to participate in a teaching program to gain experience. Seminars on selected topics and research in progress are held regularly. Opportunities are available for training in molecular biology and functional genomics, quantitative biology, bioengineering, and biomedical sciences through a variety of NIH- and USDA-sponsored interdepartmental training grants. Students are expected to complete the program in four to five years.

column46: Composition
column47: The graduate field of music at Cornell offers two distinct doctoral programs: a Ph.D. in musicology and a D.M.A. in composition. The Ph.D. program is designed for students who wish to pursue a career in teaching and scholarship. The D.M.A. program is intended for composers who wish to teach in a college, university or conservatory. The M.F.A. in composition is no longer offered for admission.

column46: Composition
column47: The graduate field of music offers three degree programs: the Ph.D. in musicology, the Doctor of Musical Arts (D.M.A.) in composition, and the Master of Fine Arts (M.F.A.) in composition. These programs provide a broad foundation in music history, theory, and performance practices. Ph.D. students specialize in historical musicology or in ethnomusicology. D.M.A. and M.F.A. students specialize in composition.

column46: ['historical musicology', 'ethnomusicology', 'composition']
column47: The graduate field of music offers three concentrations: historical musicology, ethnomusicology, and composition. The Ph.D. in musicology (historical musicology and ethnomusicology) prepares students for careers in scholarship and teaching at the university level. The D.M.A. in composition provides composers with the opportunity to develop their creative and intellectual potential to the fullest. The program is flexible and accommodates students with a wide range of interests. Students benefit from an exceptionally strong music faculty and the extensive resources of one of the world’s great research universities, including an outstanding music library. They are encouraged to pursue in-depth studies in a variety of areas of music scholarship and performance, as well as opportunities for collaborative and interdisciplinary research projects.

column47: The Master of Professional Studies (MPS) in Natural Resources and the Environment is an interdisciplinary, one-year, course-based master’s degree that prepares students for careers in environmental management and sustainability. Students in our program are recent graduates, returned Peace Corps volunteers and career professionals from non-profit organizations, government agencies and the private sector. Through coursework, a capstone project and professional development opportunities, students acquire the knowledge, skills and networks to be leaders in the environmental field.

column47: The graduate field of natural resources and the environment addresses the coupled social-ecological dimensions of natural resource management. Students in our graduate field engage with faculty from many disciplines to learn about the biological, physical, and social aspects of natural resource use and management. Our M.S. and Ph.D. students pursue research degrees that require a final thesis or dissertation. Students have access to state-of-the-art facilities and outstanding field stations that include the Arnot Teaching and Research Forest, the Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest, the Cornell Biological Field Station at Shackelton Point, and the Shoals Marine Laboratory. Most students conduct their work in close collaboration with the New York Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit, the Cornell Center for a Sustainable Future, the Cornell Institute for Climate Smart Solutions, the Cornell Water Resources Institute, the Human Dimensions Research Unit, the Center for Conservation Social Sciences, or the Center for the Environment. Students often work closely on applied problems with the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation or other state and federal agencies and non-governmental conservation organizations.
