column47: The graduate field of natural resources and the environment addresses the coupled-social ecological dimensions of landscapes and watersheds. Research problems are complex and require interdisciplinary teams of social and biophysical scientists. Faculty in our graduate field have expertise across the social and ecological sciences. Students learn to frame, analyze, and address research questions that advance both theory and the sustainable management of natural resources.

column46: Ancient Near Eastern studies (including the Hebrew Bible), Arabic and Islamic studies, Egyptology
column47: The graduate program in Near Eastern studies provides students with the opportunity to develop an advanced, interdisciplinary understanding of the languages, literatures, history, and archaeology of the Near East. The field offers Ph.D. and terminal M.A. degree programs. Students choose to specialize in one of the following areas: Ancient Near Eastern studies (including the Hebrew Bible), Arabic and Islamic studies, or Egyptology. Within each area, students formulate a course of study and research in consultation with their Special Committee that can encompass the fields of archaeology, art history, history, languages, and literatures. Students also participate in a cross-disciplinary seminar during the first year of the program that serves as an introduction to current research and methodologies in the field. Students can obtain a minor in any of the areas of specialization within the field, or in other related fields.

The graduate field of neurobiology and behavior is a group of over 50 faculty members from more than a dozen different departments in five colleges at Cornell. The field is organized to bring together faculty and students with a common interest in neurobiology and behavior. A major goal of the field is to promote a multi-disciplinary approach to research. An equally important goal is to provide a cohesive graduate training environment that enables students to mature into first-rate scientists and colleagues, fully prepared for a career in research and teaching in either an academic or industrial environment. Students design their own curriculum in consultation with their Special Committee, in order to gain a broad background in neurobiology and behavior as well as the specialized knowledge required for their thesis research. Students are encouraged to develop a program of study that crosses traditional disciplinary boundaries. Students participate in a number of seminars and journal clubs each semester.

column46: Animal Behavior, Cellular and Molecular Neuroscience, Computational Neuroscience, Neuroethology, Systems Neuroscience
column47: The graduate field of neurobiology and behavior is one of the premier programs in the world for training in neuroscience. Our more than 100 faculty members, from more than 25 departments in 7 colleges, conduct research on all aspects of the nervous system, from molecules to behavior, in a wide range of animal species. Research is aimed at understanding the fundamental mechanisms of nervous system function and the neural basis of behavior.

column47:
The graduate field of nutritional sciences has a long and respected history at Cornell. The field is composed of over 40 faculty members from 13 academic departments with interests spanning the broad area of nutrition. The field offers Ph.D. and M.S. degrees with specializations in molecular nutrition, human nutrition, community nutrition, and international nutrition. M.S. students typically specialize in one of these areas. Students in the M.S. program are frequently self-funded or are supported through a faculty member's research grant. M.S. students must successfully complete a research project and thesis under the direction of their Special Committee.

Cornell’s Didactic Program in Dietetics (DPD) and the Dietetic Internship (DI) are both accredited by the Accreditation Council for Education in Nutrition and Dietetics (ACEND). The combined DPD/DI programs and the M.S. degree provide students with the opportunity to become registered dietitian/nutritionists (RDN). Cornell participates in the DI match for M.S. applicants who have a verification statement from an ACEND-accredited DPD program. Applicants who have not completed DPD requirements but hold a bachelor’s degree from an accredited college or university may meet the DPD requirements at Cornell as part of their M.S. degree program, then complete our Dietetic Internship.

column47: The graduate field of nutritional sciences has a distinguished history of leadership in research and education. Our faculty are engaged in a wide range of basic and applied research, using approaches that range from the molecular to the societal. Students conduct research on humans, animals, and cells to create new knowledge about health, disease, and the role of nutrition and diet. Our doctoral program trains students to become independent investigators in a wide variety of settings. Students learn how to identify important research questions and how to design, conduct, and interpret experiments to answer those questions. Upon completion of the Ph.D. program, students are well qualified to secure postdoctoral or faculty positions at research universities, research positions in government agencies or industry, or positions in public health or clinical nutrition.

column47:
The graduate field of ORIE at Cornell offers a Ph.D. degree, two research-oriented M.S. degrees, and a professional M.Eng. degree.

The M.S. degrees are intended primarily for students who are interested in a research-oriented degree that might lead on to a Ph.D. degree. The Ph.D. program is for students who plan a career in research and teaching. The M.Eng. program emphasizes professional practice and is intended for students who plan to work in industry. The graduate field of ORIE includes faculty from the School of ORIE, the Department of Mathematics, the Department of Computer Science, the Johnson Graduate School of Management, and the Cornell Tech campus in New York City. Cornell offers an unparalleled combination of breadth and depth of expertise in all of the core methodological areas of the field.

column47:
The graduate field of Operations Research and Information Engineering (ORIE) offers a Ph.D. program for students who are interested in pursuing an academic or research career in the field.

The ORIE Ph.D. program prepares students for a variety of careers in academia and industry. Recent graduates have been placed in ORIE, Industrial Engineering, and Business programs at leading universities, as well as in industrial research labs, the financial services industry, and consulting firms.

Students admitted to the ORIE Ph.D. program usually have an undergraduate or master’s degree in engineering, mathematics, computer science, or a physical science. We admit a small, select group of students each year. Financial assistance is available in the form of fellowships, research assistantships, and teaching assistantships. All Ph.D. students are typically fully funded for five years.

Applicants interested in the M.Eng. degree should apply to the field of Systems Engineering.

The graduate field of Performing and Media Arts (PMA) offers a Ph.D. in performance and media studies, a two-year M.F.A. in creative visual media (e.g. film, video, and new media art) or design (scenic, lighting, and costume), and a two-year M.A. in performance and media studies. A Ph.D./M.A. is not offered in creative writing or dance.

The Ph.D. in performance and media studies offers a theoretical and historical framework for studying a range of performance and media forms, with courses in theatre and performance theory, cinema and media studies, theatre history and historiography, and performance as research. Students work with an international faculty who specialize in a wide range of fields, including: film and media studies, theatre history, performance studies, sound studies, dance and movement practices, acting and directing, design, new media, and Asian performance. Ph.D. students have an opportunity to participate in the artistic life of the department and may incorporate performance practice as a component of their research. They may also take courses with graduate faculty in related fields, including but not limited to: Anthropology, Art, Art History, Asian Studies, Classics, Comparative Literature, English, German Studies, Government, Music, and Romance Studies. Cornell offers a number of graduate minors that PMA students may also pursue including: Film and Video Studies, Feminist, Gender, and Sexuality Studies, and Visual Studies.

column47: The graduate Field of Pharmacology at Cornell University is an inter-college, inter-departmental, and multi-campus program administered by the Graduate School. The research interests of the Field’s more than 50 faculty members are diverse and represent the entire spectrum of modern pharmacological sciences. Students in the Field of Pharmacology choose from one of three concentrations: Molecular and Integrative Pharmacology; Systems and Computational Pharmacology; or Pharmacology Education. Training emphasizes a combination of didactic course work, seminars and journal clubs, and original laboratory research. The research project is the most important element of the training, and students select a research preceptor and a project during their first year of study.

column46: Systems, Molecular, and Cellular Pharmacology
column47: The graduate field of pharmacology provides research training focused on understanding the molecular mechanisms of drug action and the basis of disease. As such, it is an integrative discipline that bridges biomedical and clinical sciences. Research in the field of pharmacology uses all the tools of modern biology, from molecular and cellular to organismal, to investigate how chemical agents, both natural and synthetic, affect biological systems. These studies can provide the basis for the rational design of new therapies and the safer, more effective use of existing medicines.

column47: The graduate program in philosophy is designed to provide the training and the opportunity to do original research in philosophy. It leads to the Ph.D. degree; the M.A. is a degree in course. Admission is to the Ph.D. program. A central part of the program is a series of nine graduate seminars the student is required to take in the first three years of study. In addition to general seminars, in which a variety of topics may be discussed, the offerings are in the main areas of philosophy: metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, logic, and history of philosophy. Seminars are also offered in aesthetics, political philosophy, philosophy of mind, philosophy of language, philosophy of science, and philosophy of religion. Graduate students are encouraged to take advantage of the many courses of instruction and other intellectual activities in the department and the University that are relevant to their interests.
